Bottle fed brushes are siphon fed, which means that they generally (but not always) require higher operating pressures, correct alignment of the siphon to ensure proper feeding of paint, and can (but not always) use more paint.

Siphons/bottle feeds also depend on having a certain MINIMUM amount of paint in order for the feed to work. This means that any batch of paint you custom mix either (1) has to be used up in that single session, or (2) must be stored in an airtight container until the next session. This is not a problem if you spray paints without thinning and out of the bottle, but it's much more inconvenient if you spray a custom mix of thinned paint. Some modelers, even if they know the proper mixing ratios for a particular thinned paint, like to use the same batch because they know that mixed batch will be consistent with itself, but not necessarily with another batch mixed to identical proportions.

People use gravity feeds because they operate with lower pressures and can use a tiny drop or two of paint. For example, I used to use bottle feed. I usually had to use several milliliters of paint and thinner to meet the threshold for the bottle feed. Gravity feed (in a clean brush, mind) requires nothing more than a few drops into the paint channel and some thinner, and that should be enough.

Unless you're coating large sections of a model, you're rarely going to fill that paint reservoir anyway. I use inexpensive airbrushes made in a certain country, and find them serviceable (but seriously, get a better one if you can afford it). The first one I bought had a pretty large cup (4 or 5 ccs, I think). The latest one? I bought a 2cc cup because honestly, I *never* spray enough paint to fill it anyway, so why bother?

There are people who use bottle feeds and can get great results. Gravity feed is just a bit easier to use in my opinion. However, either one is fine.

My general order of assembly of the cockpit: 

1. Paint the instrument panel whatever color it's supposed to be. 
2. Paint the cockpit tub whatever color(s) it's supposed to be. 
3. Pick out controls with silver/white highlights, detail paint the controls looking at reference photos where possible, use graphite dust as a highlighter where appropriate. 
4. Put future floor polish mixed with the relevant clear color in the radar displays (it's not 100% accurate since powered off screens are black, but it's interesting to look at and a nice effect.) 
5. Gloss coat ALL of the cockpit surfaces where decals will be placed.
6. Decal the instrument panel. If it's supposed to conform over bumps and knobs and actual surface detail, make sure to use decal setting solution or it won't stick properly.
7. Wait for the decal to dry. Then flat coat if appropriate. 
8. Drop using a very small brush, future into the "glass" dials of the instrument panel. 

**The instrument panel should be decaled as a separate part where possible (easier to do it that way, since you'll have the most access to it) and then glued to the final cockpit tub. 

Your order is fine. I would leave the instrument panel OFF if it's separate, because it'll make it easier to place the decals (on a flat surface) instead of trying to wedge it into an already assembled cockpit.

Plastic: a popular brand of extra thin cement, a well-known solvent adhesive, a common liquid cement (it's liquid, not any kind of "gel"), and although I haven't used it personally, a specific bonding agent for plastic. Of the list, I particularly prefer the extra thin cement and the solvent adhesive. Both are *not* non-toxic, and most solvent-based plastic glues are not nontoxic. All of these work on the principle of providing a solvent that melts the plastic and fuses the two parts to be joined together. It works ONLY for compatible plastics, most particularly for the polystyrene in plastic kits. Because these all dissolve plastic, NONE of them are non-toxic, and all of them have highly chemical smells to them.

The non-toxic glue you're using does not use that kind of solvent, which is why it's non-toxic. As you've discovered, it also doesn't stick things together very well.

When using liquid cement, be aware: this stuff will get everywhere, and you are advised to use it sparingly. The liquid cement (particularly the extra thin version, but a thicker version in an orange bottle is also available) includes a brush integrated into the cap. If you ever drop a drop of this stuff onto a plastic surface, DO NOT touch it with your fingers, as the solvent will soften the plastic and leave fingerprint marks if you touch that area. Perhaps remove it with a tissue or something.

How to use liquid cement: when joining surfaces such as fuselages, it's more like "flowing" the stuff into the gap and letting capillary action do the rest.

Wood: a common wood cement, a popular wood glue, PVA wood glue, and rare but still available, a specific type of cement for wood.

The airbrush I use costs about that much. There are some compromises.

1. They are definitely not precision machined, at least, no more than is absolutely necessary. Expect less precision, more slop, and not as finely polished surfaces. (In fact, if I were to buy another one, the first thing I'd do is open it up, disassemble it, lube and polish all parts I think would interfere with the trigger and valve).

2. They need to be kept religiously clean and require more maintenance per session. Why? My theory is that the less precise, rougher machining (and some design flaws) make it easier for paint to catch onto rough surfaces of the nozzle, needle, and tip, making tip dry a bigger problem than with other brushes that are more expensively lined.

3. Are they serviceable? If you keep them religiously clean, clean them and strip it down each session (the nozzle, needle, tip, nozzle head), then they work just fine. But if you don't clean it, it will jam a lot faster than everything else.

4. Spare parts are "expensive" relative to the cost of the brush. It's rarely ever worth it to say, buy a new needle; you might as well buy a new brush and have some spare parts.

A setting solution is supposed to help it lay down flat, yes, but on a glossy surface, it's even better.

You can keep sanding and polishing, and it *will* help. But a gloss coat will be an easier solution, as long as you weren't too rough with your initial color paintwork.

2. Then, the simple solution: spray a gloss coat, wait to dry, or use a specific floor polish as your "surface preparation" before placing the decal. 

3. The setting solution DOES help, but you're missing the point. The reason why you have silvering problems on a matte finish is because the paint (if you magnify it with a microscope or magnifying glass) is because the texture is not nearly as smooth as a good gloss paint would have on it. 

Everything everyone else said so far about air bubbles is sound. The reason why decals silver is because there are microbubbles trapped underneath the decal. The preparation is supposed to help probably break surface tension and try to "suck in" the decals to the microbubbles. However, think about it. What's easier to do? Doing that to a smooth surface, or a micro-pebbly one made by the matte paint/sealer? The solvent, when applied after the decal is placed, will also help it conform and partially deals with the problem, but it won't "push out" air bubbles that are already trapped there.

The solvent should generally be applied only after the decal has been placed in final position. There's a reason for this. Once you put on the solvent, you should not move the decal at all, and it might even wrinkle as it's drying. The wrinkles will almost always settle themselves out as the decal gets more tightly pasted to the surface. Touch that decal, and it might disintegrate, turn into a melted mess, or what have you.

If you ever have a chance, compare the dried texture of matte paint versus gloss paint. You'll notice a very distinct difference. One will be "rougher" than the other.

10. Weather.

That is a technique commonly used by many modelers right now called "preshading." 

What you're seeing is a primer coat of a light gray color, with a dark color sprayed along areas of either (1) shadow, (2) along panel lines of the model, (3) maintenance and access panels of the model. 

The reason this is done is because those areas will look slightly different than the other areas of the model. On some models, panels that are regularly removed have a slightly different (darker or lighter) shade than the rest of what would otherwise be a uniformly colored piece. This effect is more noticeable on some models than others (look for example at a specific military aircraft and you'll see the shading differences). This is designed to emulate that. 

Here, I'm doing this mostly because it adds a bit of color contrast, even if it's not particularly faithful to scale, because a monotone model can be visually boring to look at. 

After the dark color dries, you spray the final color coats over it, while spraying the paint thin enough to leave the dark color somewhat visible underneath it. The final effect creates some shading variations along what would otherwise be a uniform color, and also, in the way I'm doing it, provides some emphasis to the control surfaces of the model and its hinges (those lines along the back edge of the wings and stabilizer).

The use of the technique is currently widely accepted, particularly in model making publications and media. There is some backlash against using it, with the most colorful comparison I've heard likening it to someone wearing too much makeup and appearing gaudy or overdone.

In this case, I'm using this as a testbed because it's a quick and painless build for me, compared to some of the projects I am working on that are comparatively more tedious; it's also an experiment to see if shading the panels in blue and then applying the final color will create an appealing contrast.

Here's an example of a real-world photo of models that could benefit from preshading, featuring a military aircraft and another fighter jet.

Note that this effect can be easily overdone, but in some cases, it might still be worthwhile. Personally, I think it's often overdone and looks garish if not executed properly. Here's an example of it being overdone (from a well-known model manufacturer's own promotional photos). Look at those black bands around the various panels of the airframe. That's when it's overdone. Also, you have to spend a ton of money doing research, getting the CAD drawings, getting someone to make you small batches of the valve gear for steam engines, die casting bits, and everything else.

Tooling actually used to cost more; if you look at the recent explosion of startup manufacturers of plastic model kits, that suggests tooling costs are less than they used to be, but even then, they are horrendously expensive.

Is it possible that some manufacturers are also trying to maximize their profits? Yes, sure. But you're ignoring that these things aren't cheap, certainly not at the volumes you're seeing them being sold today. Model trains are not a common hobby among children, not like it was in the 50s and 60s.

Further, there's also the size of the production batch that matters. Preshade versus black basing:

1. *Differences in level of precision required*: Preshade requires more precision (e.g., you paint in the panel lines you want shaded), versus black bases - paint the whole thing in black, then paint in the color of the model selectively with dots of sprayed paint. Can you or your airbrush paint straight lines? Then preshade and postshade is arguably quicker.

2. *Speed of painting/comparison*: Preshading is quicker if you're a precise painter, while black bases are much more tedious to do, but easier if you can't paint straight lines. Black bases (depending on how executed) can also offer a bit more room for tonal variation for less effort on the backend (because of the way you fill in the black areas with the base color).

3. *The processes are not as different as they seem, just arguably in reverse*: They are somewhat opposite processes to reach the same result. I've used both. It really depends on what you're trying to do, but you can get very similar effects using either. I don't think it leads to some amazingly different result, really, it's kind of two ways to get the same tonal variation in the paint. Black basing is more tedious but offers more control because you're slowly adding in paint.

4. *Selected advantages/disadvantages*: Finally, one disadvantage of pre-shading is that for the panel lines you don't shade in, if you're only painting in the base color, then it assumes that your center panels will be a nearly uniform color.

5. *Guys, pin washing is nothing "new" it's just a new name to refer to something that's been in use for decades, and by guys who want to sell you stuff*: Really, this current trend of calling it pin-washing was invented by major weathering experts or weathering product companies recently to name a technique that is decades old (I'd say time immemorial, but I'm not nearly that old, thankfully); or a well-known figure in the modeling community may have coined the term. (To be clear, I don't have any real problem with weathering products, they are wonderful things; it's just that too often people seem to think these things are cure-alls for lack of practice or that a well weathered/built subject is just a question of what *product* to buy).

6. *But wait, if you do preshading and post-shading you can get a similar result to black basing*: But you can solve that with post-shading, e.g., lightened or darkened versions of the base paint to introduce the same tonal variation you'd see with black basing.

7. *Get off my damn lawn, it's just using a panel line wash/what it does*: Pin washing...back in my day we just called it an oil/panel line wash. I always use it. It's a means of adding shadow, depth, and emphasizing panel lines that wouldn't be as visible on scaled down models and also makes engraved detail pop. You should do it almost as a matter of course.

Masking canopies is tedious as all hell. Next time you buy a model kit from a certain manufacturer, buy a more advanced version; it'll include photoetched parts occasionally, sometimes some resin, and most importantly for your purposes, a canopy mask set which is tape that is precut to shape.

What I use for canopy masking is a specific brand of tape (you can also use self-adhesive foil), and then, with a brand new, razor-sharp blade, I use the blade to cut through the tape. It's a delicate job; you need only apply enough force to feel a certain "click" or sensation that you've punched through the paper, and that's all. Regular tape is too thick for this application, and the specific brand of tape is thinner and more tolerant of handling.

It's a tedious, boring, and annoyingly irritating task that is totally unforgiving and requires that you be absolutely precise. Also, you need to be gentle, or you'll scratch the glass. To be blunt, an entire model that is otherwise perfectly executed can be completely ruined or rendered pointless by a damaged canopy. Unless you're building something where it logically wouldn't be there (like a wreck). These days, I find the exercise so tedious and annoying that for anything below 1/48 scale, I seriously would purchase masks for all of those, and above 1/48 scale, even then, given my limited hobby time, it's actually worth my money to pay for the masks.

Also, I emphasize that you need a NEW or razor-sharp blade for this.

As the damage issues have been extensively covered here, consider the following as general points of improvement (well, also some points about the damage)

1. The paint is applied quite thickly, and the masking could be greatly improved. How I can tell is that you can see the large demarcation line between the two colors, so thick, in fact, that you can see a layer of paint as a "step" above. This suggests you either (1) didn't thin your paints adequately, or (2) used too many layers to get a fairly thick, if solid colored coat of paint. 

2. That decal is already peeling off, which would not happen on the real thing because that would likely have been painted on. Decals should be applied after a gloss coat is applied to the surface to prevent silvering (which will happen on flat paint, and if it doesn't, you got lucky) due to micro air bubbles trapped underneath the decal. You can use a soft cloth in order to press down the decal once it's in the final position. In this case, it's just plain peeling off. You can use either a spray can, or a common clear liquid product which can also be used to coat the canopy. You can then, after applying decals, hand brush a coat of a specific acrylic flat clear, which is brushable compared to many other flat coats.

3. Paint generally speaking across the entire model is thick, and has visible brush strokes. Use a wider brush (around 1/4 inch or so, for a smaller model, maybe larger for a bigger model), flat headed, and work on a wet edge (i.e. don't repeatedly go over the same area you already painted, because that will leave brush marks; that's what multiple layers are for). 

4. You should work on your transitions between the different flying surfaces. On the tail, you can see where one color has bled onto the other side of the fin. For detail work in areas like that, use a thin brush, or very carefully use the fin's edge to your favor. Either way, you could've also touched it up with pinpoints of paint from a toothpick. 

5. Aircraft, even these, are not solid sheets of metal, and have longerons and ribs inside the fuselage. If you're going to blow holes through the fuselage, be mindful of where the ribbing would be. Most of the damage photos posted have strips of metal protruding from them or trailing them, because of this kind of construction structure. This effect is particularly unconvincing in the middle of the wing, which in most aircraft is largely either strips of metal, or hollow space, or fuel tanks. Bullet holes or shrapnel damage is closer to what you're going for, but even then, look at references.

6. You should mask your canopies, as that painting up front is quite messy, even in the most charitable terms. 

7. You also treat the damage as if it would look essentially identical no matter where on the aircraft it hit. That isn't how it would work, because of the differing methods of construction for various parts, thickness of the metal, whether any vital components were in the area or equipment, etc. 

Finally, as a global comment to the damage...the damage aside from the holes looks like...well, silver paint spattered at random intervals. Bullets would've torn and damaged the metal, ripped holes in it, took bits of it through the rest of the structure, create shrapnel that causes other damage, etc. Overall, this isn't a terrible model, but it certainly could've been much better, even given that you don't use an airbrush. There are two schools of thought I've run into:

1. One perspective suggests that panel line washes should always be applied as a matter of artistic interpretation of the full-size subject. Honestly, many current trends in heavy weathering, shading, and very dark panel line washes often seem somewhat divorced from reality when compared to reference photos. Some aircraft (especially those from wealthier air forces or those that undergo more maintenance, or presumably are stored in closed hangars) can exhibit surprisingly little weathering, while older and less well-maintained airframes may show significant wear. For instance, if you examine various photos of a specific fighter jet model, you'll notice considerable variation. Some appear to have no visible panel lines or only very faint ones, while others look as dark as models do. This approach highlights that, as scale models, lighting and other factors do not scale with the subject, so it's perfectly acceptable to include washes and dark ones, as well as unusual color fading to create something *interesting to look at.* The current trend popularized by various modeling brands tends to lean towards this viewpoint (plus they are also trying to sell their products; nothing wrong with that, as they are useful and convenient, but keep in mind they have a vested interest in encouraging you to emulate their models).

2. The other perspective focuses on examining references and considering other issues that do not scale. For example, if you look at the gun port of a specific fighter jet, you'll see that it's black because of a vent or similar feature. On the model, if you *don't* apply a black or dark brown wash there, the shadow of the vent won't be visible on the model because shadows do not scale the same way they do on the real aircraft. This school of thought argues that washes and similar effects should be based primarily or even exclusively on available reference materials that indicate where wear and tear occurs.

Additionally, be aware that there are pristine aircraft and very dirty ones, so what may be appropriate for one airplane may not be for another.

As a further aside, the current trend towards preshading in black, and more recently, what is referred to as "black basing," was practically unused during the late 90s and early 2000s. It's a relatively new and trendy technique.

Similarly, referring to something as a "pin wash" is just a term coined by certain respected modelmakers and product sellers who found a new way to describe a process that has been used for a long time. Other terms, like "oil paint rendering," "dot filters," "filters," "modulation," etc., are largely the creations of individuals in the modeling community (perhaps not one specific person). One notable figure specifically coined the term "oil paint rendering" in their publications (abbreviating it as "OPR," likely to avoid repeatedly typing "oil paint rendering" in their book).

There are also some individuals who choose a middle ground. I create my artwork for visual interest and with reference to images, but I typically don't go to great lengths to depict the wear patterns on a specific model.

Instead, my work often involves (1) creating tonal variation for visual appeal, (2) a combination of reference images that are usually not limited to a single aircraft and applying washes and weathering that are common to the type based on those images, while also considering elements that don't scale (like vent holes for weaponry).

1. Adding more layers (particularly on vehicle models, where paint essentially has to be perfect) almost never solves an undercoat problem. If your previous coat was bad (i.e. it wasn't a mist coat that wasn't designed to cover everything in a gloss candy finish all at once), adding more layers really just adds more things to go wrong. 

2. Primer isn't supposed to be gloss, but what it *is* supposed to be is smooth. Like satin to the touch, ideally, or just dead flat. The point of it is to create an even substrate to apply the final coats to, so if it's pebbly your final coat had better be really thick, or it's going to show. Pebbly primer will show on thin/mist coats and probably even after a "wet" coat.

Several points. 

1. Decals that aren't specifically stated as being produced by reputable manufacturers are notoriously thick and difficult to work with. 

2. What you have is "silvering" of the decals, not as a result of application of the dull coat. That's the result of surface imperfections on the painted surface or the surface the decal is applied to that results in what essentially is imperfect adhesion of the decal to the surface. 

3. For decals to look painted on, surface preparation is everything. What you need to apply is a gloss coat prior to application of decals. Some people skip it occasionally, but that's basically a gamble that your finish is smooth enough not to cause the microbubble problem. Your model is brush painted. 

4. The main way to avoid this outline problem is to avoid having it in the first place. It's very difficult to fix. One method is to try to soak it with decal setting solvents, or carefully poking holes in the decal with the point of a knife blade (hard to do without denting the paintwork) and then flooding the area with solvent.

Actually, painting camouflage is pretty standard practice for most aircraft modelers, particularly those who don't model military aircraft, since those tend to be variations of gray, gray, and oh yeah, gray. 

It certainly does not require oil paints to accomplish (if anything, that's the first I've heard of anyone trying to create gradients using oil paints with their accompanying slow drying time for a camouflage scheme). What it *does* take is either good work with a brush using three different colors or masking work using rolls of putty or an intricately cut mask for the various areas. 

Typically, this is done in layers, starting with the lightest color on the whole model first and finishing with the darkest color last. 

As for the original poster, if you're planning to brush paint this, I would not suggest certain popular paint brands. They're much more suited for use with an airbrush.

Aftermarket solutions aren't going to fix your problem. The issue is that your surface preparation isn't smooth enough to allow for good decal adhesion. If you want to go aftermarket, you'll need to strip all the decals and paint and redo it. The problem lies with the surface you applied it to, not the decal itself. As poor as some decals can be, they *do* work.

You need a good gloss coat, an even coat of paint underneath that, and for good measure, a decal setting solution like a popular brand or another well-known option (I'd avoid the strongest one, as it's too intense for most applications.)
